question: In recent years it has come to light that major banks – including Danske Bank, Jyske Bank and Nordea – have had serious problems when it comes to the collection of debt from their most vulnerable customers in Denmark and other European countries123.

Over-payments relating to debt collection apparently stem from a number of serious system and data errors in banks’ debt collection systems that keep track of bad payers. The systems have overstated customers’ debts, collected debts from the wrong customers and collected debts, fees and interest that are outdated and therefore cannot legally be collected4.

In addition, an urgent review at Danske Bank carried out by the bank’s own internal audit department shows that the debt department and parts of Danske Bank’s management have been aware of the problems for several years, and yet no substantial changes have been made to the bank’s debt collection practices5. 1.

What is the Commission’s view of the fact that several major banks operating throughout the EU appear to be able to get away with not taking legitimate and timely action in cases where there is a risk of vulnerable citizens overpaying banks in debt collection procedures?
Will the Commission look into ways of tightening up the enforcement of the rules governing lawful debt collection by banks operating within the European Union?
answer: The Union has a comprehensive bank regulatory and supervisory framework to ensure banks’ practices towards customers are sound business practices. The Capital Requirements Directive (CRD) (6) requires banks to have adequate internal control mechanisms that promote sound and effective risk management.

It also tasks supervisors to ensure that administration and monitoring of the banks’ portfolios, including identifying and managing credits' problems, is operated via effective systems. In mortgage lending, the Mortgage Credit Directive requires creditors to exercise reasonable forbearance before foreclosure proceedings are initiated (7).

In consumer credit lending, the Consumer Credit Directive (CCD) (8) requires creditors to put in place forbearance measures (including modifications of the terms and conditions, e.g. extending the term, changing its type or reducing the payment rate, or a total or partial refinancing of the initial credit agreement), when appropriate.

The CRD empowers supervisors to annually assess the arrangements, strategies, processes and mechanisms implemented by banks to comply with the EU regulatory framework. It also provides supervisors with enforcement powers to ensure banks take the necessary measures.

Enforcing the EU regulatory framework for credit institutions is primarily the competence of the supervisory authorities, including the Single Supervisory Mechanism for certain large banks in the Union. The European Banking Authority has issued guidelines to further steer the work of supervisors and banks in the application of the EU rules. The revision of the CRD (9) will clarify and further strengthen the internal control and risk management requirements.
